blocks.text: A standard deviation is a measure of how dispersed the data is in relation to the mean. Low, or small, standard deviation indicates data are clustered tightly around the mean, and high, or large, standard deviation indicates data are more spread out. A standard deviation close to zero indicates that data points are very close to the mean, whereas a larger standard deviation indicates data points are spread further away from the mean.

blocks.alt: Two red bell-shaped curves on black baselines. Curve (a) is wide and low; curve (b) is narrow and tall. In each a green line marks the mean (mu) at the peak and a second green line one standard deviation (sigma) away, with a double arrow labelled sigma between them. Under the curves: a) The curve is more spread out and has a high standard deviation; b) The curve is more clustered around the mean and has a lower standard deviation.
blocks.caption: Normal curves: (a) more spread out, high standard deviation; (b) more clustered around the mean, lower standard deviation (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure).

blocks.text: In biology, standard deviation is commonly used to assess the variability in measurements, such as the growth rates of plants, the concentration of enzymes in a sample, or any other biological data.

items: xᵢ = each individual data point in the set
N = total number of data points.

blocks.text: Steps to calculate Standard Deviation with example
A biologist studied the heights of 9 different plants of the same species. The heights of the plants are 56cm, 65cm, 74cm, 75cm, 76cm, 77cm, 80cm, 81cm and 91cm.

items: Step2: Subtract the mean from each data point to find the deviation of each point.
Step3: Square the result of each deviation which eliminates negative values and emphasizes larger deviations.
Step4: Find the average of the squared deviations.
Step5: Take the square root of the result from step 4. This is the standard deviation.

blocks.caption: Table: Calculation of standard deviation for plant heights
header: Subtract mean from each data point (xᵢ - µ)
Square the result of each deviation (xᵢ - µ)²
Variance (Average of the squared deviations) ∑(xᵢ - µ)²/N
